sheet.title: Steak Tartare with Rye
sheet.replaces: The Steak Tartare Cannoli (d-0w2k5cdm), which moves to the past menu items.
ingredients: Tartare Dressing (egg yolk, dijon, caper, shallot, hot sauce, parsley, black pepper)
Montreal Seasoning (Black pepper, carraway, coriander, chili flake, mustard seed)
chefFacts: Montreal steak spice originated in the 1940s at Schwartz's Hebrew Delicatessan when a cook used his deli's traditional smoked-meat pickling spices on a steak for his lunch
In the late 1800's, steak tartare was originally called beefsteak a L'Americaine before a version was created by Auguste Escoffier using tartar sauce, leading to the name a la tartare
Vital Farms is a collection of small egg farms that share practices of ethical farming
Rye is a grain which is closely related to wheat known for its earthy, nutty flavor
sheet.note: As printed, spelling included (Delicatessan, carraway, a L'Americaine). The printed heading names the chef; here he is the chef. The sheet prints no price, no cut, no portion, no recipe and no word on whether the yolk is raw. The allergen list is the same, word for word, as the October sheet's, and it belongs in the service note only.

chefFacts.fact: Montreal steak spice originated in the 1940s at Schwartz's Hebrew Delicatessan when a cook used his deli's traditional smoked-meat pickling spices on a steak for his lunch
chefFacts.whatSourcesSay: This is the story Montreal tells, and two sources carry it, but it is the deli's lore and not a dated record. The account: a broilerman at Schwartz's, known as The Shadow, working there in the 1940s and 1950s, began putting the deli's smoked meat pickling spices on his own rib and liver steaks; customers asked for the same, and other Montreal delis and steakhouses took it up. CBC credits the same man with popularizing the mix and counts more than 70 years of it, yet says only he knows the real origins. Schwartz's own history page tells of the 1928 founding and the smoked meat and does not tell this story. So the place and the pickling spice link stand; the date is a pair of decades, the 1940s and 1950s, not a year; and 'for his lunch' is the sheet's way of saying his own steaks. The deli's formal name is the Montreal Hebrew Delicatessen. Beside the chef's words: the sources agree on Schwartz's and the smoked meat spices and put it in the 1940s and 1950s; nobody has a record of the day.

chefFacts.fact: In the late 1800's, steak tartare was originally called beefsteak a L'Americaine before a version was created by Auguste Escoffier using tartar sauce, leading to the name a la tartare
chefFacts.whatSourcesSay: The name history stands; 'created by Escoffier' does not. Britannica puts raw chopped beef on a few French bistro and restaurant menus in the late 19th century under the name à l'Américaine, in the American style, presumably because the French believed Americans ate meat raw (Wikipedia dates the name to the early twentieth century). Escoffier's Le Guide Culinaire of 1903 prints both dishes: Beefsteak à l'Américaine, chopped fillet with a raw egg yolk and with capers, onion and parsley apart, and Beefsteak à la Tartare, the same without the yolk, with tartar sauce served on the side. So the name does come from the sauce: steak à la tartare means steak served with tartar sauce, later shortened to steak tartare. What no source shows is that Escoffier created that version. His book records it, and a Hamburg steak à la tartare was already in print in The Epicurean of 1894, the book of a New York restaurant chef. The turn worth knowing: the tartare served today, with the yolk, is Escoffier's à l'Américaine wearing the other dish's name. By the Larousse Gastronomique of 1938, steak tartare meant raw beef with a raw yolk and no tartar sauce at all. Beside the chef's words: Escoffier wrote both versions down in 1903; the sauce gave the name; nobody can name the inventor.

chefFacts.fact: Vital Farms is a collection of small egg farms that share practices of ethical farming
chefFacts.whatSourcesSay: A fair short form, as long as nobody hears a farmers' cooperative. Vital Farms is a company: founded in 2007 near Austin, Texas, with 20 hens, its shares on the Nasdaq since 2020, a Certified B Corporation. It keeps no single great flock. It buys from a network of contracted small family farms, 575 of them by its own count in November 2025 and more than 600 by the end of that year, each held to the company's pasture-raised standard: at least 108 square feet of outdoor pasture a hen, the Certified Humane figure. So the farms do share one set of practices, because the company sets it. One thing a server needs from the producer's own page: Vital Farms says its eggs in the shell are not pasteurized.

chefFacts.fact: Rye is a grain which is closely related to wheat known for its earthy, nutty flavor
chefFacts.whatSourcesSay: Rye, Secale cereale, sits in the same grass tribe as wheat and barley, the Triticeae, and is close enough to wheat that the two cross: the hybrid is triticale. A flour miller describes its flavor as earthy and malty; 'nutty' is common tasting language that today's sources did not print, so earthy is the sourced word. Two things to add at the table. The anise-like taste people call rye in a deli loaf is caraway seed, not the grain, and caraway is in this plate's Montreal seasoning, so the tuile and the spice echo each other. And rye is a gluten grain, lower in gluten than wheat but not without it; the sheet marks Gluten, and dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

origin.text: France, on restaurant and bistro menus, from the late 19th century (Britannica) or the early twentieth (Wikipedia), under the name beefsteak à l'Américaine. The first firmly documented recipe is in Escoffier's Le Guide Culinaire, 1903. In English the words steak tartare are first recorded in 1911, and by the Larousse Gastronomique of 1938 the name meant the dish known today: raw beef with a raw egg yolk.

name.text: Tartare is the French for Tartar, the old European name for the Tatar peoples of Central Asia; the word came into French from Medieval Latin Tartarus, a reshaping of Persian Tātār. On a French menu à la tartare first meant 'with tartar sauce', and steak à la tartare was shortened to steak tartare. The tale that Tatar or Mongol horsemen tenderized raw meat under their saddles and ate it is a legend: the account behind it has the meat laid under the saddle to ease the horse's sores. À l'Américaine means in the American style.

credited.text: Nobody. No source names an inventor. Auguste Escoffier (1846 to 1935) fixed both early versions in print in 1903 and is credited with recording them, not with creating them. Charles Ranhofer, the chef tied to Delmonico's in New York, had a Hamburg steak à la tartare in his book The Epicurean in 1894, nine years earlier.

story.text: Raw chopped beef began to appear on a few French bistro and restaurant menus in the late 19th century and became common in the early 20th.

Its first menu name was à l'Américaine, in the American style, presumably because popular belief in France held that Americans ate their meat raw. Wikipedia agrees on the name and places it in the early twentieth century.

The American thread is the Hamburg steak, chopped beef that was a New York fashion: the oldest English document to name it is a Delmonico's menu of 1873, and The Epicurean of 1894, by that house's chef Charles Ranhofer, prints a Hamburg steak of chopped tenderloin with an à la tartare version. One source calls that version raw; the entry itself was not read today.

Escoffier's Le Guide Culinaire of 1903 prints two neighbors. Beefsteak à l'Américaine: finely chopped fillet, a raw egg yolk on top, capers, chopped onion and parsley served apart. Beefsteak à la Tartare: the same beef without the yolk, with sauce tartare served separately. Wikipedia's steak tartare article cites the same definition from the 1921 edition, a later edition of the same book.

The tartar sauce of 1903 was not today's pickle and mayonnaise: Escoffier worked hard-boiled egg yolks to a paste, mounted them with oil and vinegar, and finished with a puree of green onion or chives and a little mayonnaise.
Steak à la tartare, literally steak served with tartar sauce, was shortened to steak tartare; Merriam-Webster's first known use of the English words is 1911.

Over time the difference between the two dishes disappeared. The Larousse Gastronomique of 1938 describes steak tartare as raw ground beef served with a raw egg yolk, with no mention of tartar sauce; a French children's encyclopedia calls that the oldest surviving recipe under the name.

So the plate a guest knows as steak tartare (chopped raw beef, a yolk, capers, onion or shallot, parsley, mustard) is the à l'Américaine build under the tartare name. Britannica gives the classic as chopped raw beefsteak bound by raw egg yolk and seasoned with mustard, capers and other ingredients.

Ours follows that classic: the seven things in the sheet's dressing are the old garnishes folded into one binder, with a second yolk served whole. What is new is the Montreal seasoning and the rye tuile in place of toast.

method.note: This is the classic as cooks make it, for understanding the plate. It is not the house recipe: the sheet prints no method, and how the kitchen cuts, dresses and plates is the chef's answer (the pack already carries those lineup asks).

steps.text: Start from a whole piece of beef, never bought mince. Tenderloin (filet) is the classic choice; French recipes name rump (rumsteck) first or beside it, and one kitchen guide allows sirloin. The sources disagree on the cut, not on the rule that it is a whole muscle cut fresh.
Trim away every bit of fat, sinew and silver skin, so nothing chewy survives into a dish that gets no cooking.
steps.basis: kitchen practice recorded in the repository's earlier dossier; not sourced again today

steps.text: Firm the beef in the freezer until it is stiff but not frozen. Recipes differ: 15 to 20 minutes, about 40, or 30 to 45. A cold, firm piece cuts cleanly and stays cold while it is worked.

Cut by hand with a sharp knife: slices, then matchsticks, then a fine, even dice of 3 to 5 mm. There are two schools, hand chopping for texture and grinding so the meat does not warm; the writers and the chef found here hand cut.
Keep it very cold the whole time: back under refrigeration between steps, at 5°C (41°F) or less, the Food Code's cold holding line.

Make the dressing. The yolk and the mustard are the binder (a yolk's lecithin is the emulsifier); into it go finely chopped shallot or onion, capers and parsley, black pepper, and the hot seasoning: a few drops of Tabasco and a dash of Worcestershire in the French classics, and in one recipe a little ketchup. The sheet's version: egg yolk, Dijon, caper, shallot, hot sauce, parsley, black pepper.

Dress at the last moment. Either fold the dressing through the beef in the kitchen, or serve it the old way Escoffier printed it: the beef plated with the yolk on top and the garnishes apart, mixed at the table.
steps.basis: the two builds are sourced; 'at the last moment' is kitchen practice from the repository's earlier dossier

steps.text: Taste, correct the seasoning, shape, set the yolk on top and serve at once with something crisp: toast or fries in a brasserie, the rye tuile here. A mixed tartare is never held or stored.

ratios.text: Beef: 150 to 200 g a person as a main course in the French recipes found (600 g of rump for four in one, 200 g for one in another). A starter is smaller; the house portion is not printed.

For four: 2 shallots, 4 tablespoons of chopped flat parsley, 1 to 2 tablespoons of capers, 2 tablespoons of Dijon mustard, a dash of Worcestershire sauce and a few drops of Tabasco (optional); one recipe adds 2 tablespoons of ketchup.
Caution on all four: these are orders of magnitude from general recipe pages, not from Larousse or Escoffier (the 1903 page gives no weights in what was read), and not the house's proportions.

temps.text: Cold holding: 5°C (41°F) or less, FDA Food Code 3-501.16.
Freezer firming before the cut: 15 to 45 minutes, firm but not frozen (recipes differ).
There is no cooking step. The USDA's kill step for ground beef is 160°F, and a tartare never gets it, which is why the dish is served only at the guest's choice and under the consumer advisory.
The first pick wine is poured at 55 to 58°F (the pack's figure, not researched again here).

faults.cause: Put through a grinder or chopped until it warms, so the cut edges smear instead of staying clean dice.
faults.basis: the hand cut preference is sourced; 'pasty and gray' is the repository's earlier kitchen note

faults.cause: Not firmed in the cold before cutting, or left out between steps.
Sinew or silver skin left in, or a dice cut too large.
Mixed ahead and held. A dressed tartare is made to order and never stored.
faults.basis: sourced (one weak source, plus the repository note on seasoning at the last moment)

faults.fault: All mustard and heat, no beef
faults.cause: Too heavy a hand with the Dijon, hot sauce or spice hides a mild cut; pairing writers make the same point about wine, that a tartare is easily overwhelmed.
faults.basis: kitchen judgment; the wine parallel is sourced

faults.cause: A tuile is crisp because it is thin and rich in fat; one that has picked up moisture bends instead of snapping.
faults.basis: what makes a tuile crisp is sourced; the fault is kitchen knowledge, not sourced today

components.name: Raw beef tenderloin
components.what: The tenderloin is the long, lean muscle along the inside of the backbone, the most tender cut on the animal because it does almost no work; the Chateaubriand is its thick center. Here the sheet prints it plainly as raw.
components.how: In the classic: trimmed of all sinew, firmed in the cold, cut by hand to a fine dice and dressed to order. How this kitchen cuts it and the portion are not printed.
components.tastes: Cool, soft and silky, with a mild, clean beef flavor and little fat.
components.why: With no cooking to soften anything, tenderness has to come from the cut itself, and tenderloin's fine grain gives a dice that melts. Its mildness is the trade: French recipes often name rump first for more flavor, and the mild cut is why the dressing and the spice do the talking on this plate.

components.name: The hand cut (the knife technique behind a tartare)
components.what: A tartare is a knife cut before it is a recipe: slices, then matchsticks, then a small even dice, 3 to 5 mm.
components.how: The beef is firmed in the freezer for 15 to 45 minutes so the knife cuts clean, then diced and kept very cold.
components.tastes: Texture, not flavor: separate, tender little cubes instead of a paste.
components.why: Cooks split into two schools, hand cutting for texture and grinding to keep the meat cool; the sources found here hand cut. Merriam-Webster's definition still says ground beef, so a guest may expect mince. How ours is cut is a lineup ask the pack already carries.

components.name: Tartare dressing (egg yolk, Dijon, caper, shallot, hot sauce, parsley, black pepper)
components.what: The seasoning that turns chopped beef into the dish: the garnishes Escoffier sent to the table apart in 1903 (yolk, capers, onion, parsley), here folded into one dressing with mustard, pepper and hot sauce.
components.how: Yolk and Dijon are stirred into a glossy binder (the yolk's lecithin is an emulsifier), and the finely chopped capers, shallot and parsley go in with the pepper and the hot sauce. Proportions, and whether it is mixed through or served beside, are the chef's.
components.tastes: Rich from the yolk, sharp from the mustard, briny from the capers, gently oniony from the shallot, fresh from the parsley, warm from the pepper and the hot sauce.
components.why: Lean raw beef needs fat, salt, acid and bite, and this gives all four. It is not tartar sauce: that is a cold sauce of the mayonnaise family, and the shared name is history, not recipe. Egg is in this dressing as well as in the separate yolk, so a question about one is a question about both and goes to the kitchen.

components.name: Dijon mustard (in the dressing)
components.what: The smooth, pale, sharp French mustard: brown mustard seed with white wine and vinegar. The name is a style, not a protected place.
components.how: Stirred raw into the yolk, never heated here, so its bite stays whole.
components.tastes: Smooth and sharp. Mustard's pungency comes from isothiocyanates, released when the seed is crushed and wetted.
components.why: It is the binder's second half and the classic sharp note against rich yolk and mild beef; the mustard seed in the Montreal seasoning repeats it in whole spice form.

components.name: Capers, shallot and parsley (in the dressing)
components.what: Capers are the cured flower buds of Capparis spinosa; shallot is the small, fine-flavored cousin of the onion; parsley is the fresh green. The pack already has a card for each.
components.how: All three chopped fine and raw.
components.tastes: Briny and tangy; gently sharp and sweet; grassy and clean.
components.why: They are the oldest companions of the dish: capers, onion and parsley are the three garnishes on Escoffier's 1903 page.

components.name: Hot sauce and black pepper (in the dressing)
components.what: Two kinds of warmth. In the French classic the hot sauce is a few drops of Tabasco, with Worcestershire beside it; the sheet says only hot sauce, and which one is the chef's answer.
components.how: A few drops stirred into the dressing; pepper ground in.
components.tastes: Vinegar-bright chili heat at the front of the mouth from the sauce; slower, warmer heat at the back from the pepper.
components.why: A little acid and heat wake up a rich, cold dish. For a spice-shy guest the level is a kitchen question, since chili also sits in the Montreal seasoning.

components.name: Montreal seasoning (black pepper, caraway, coriander, chili flake, mustard seed)
components.what: The steak spice of Montreal's smoked meat delis, here in the house's own five: black pepper, caraway, coriander, chili flake and mustard seed. The well-known commercial blend is different: garlic, coriander, black pepper, cayenne flakes, dill seed and salt. Blends vary by maker, and at least one sold blend does carry caraway.
components.how: A dry blend of cracked and whole spices, traditionally the pickling spice rub of smoked meat, shaken over steak. How coarse the house grinds it, and whether it is folded in or dusted over, is not printed.
components.tastes: Peppery and aromatic: warm pepper, the rye-bread note of caraway, the lemony lift of coriander, a prickle of chili and the sharp pop of mustard seed. The printed five carry no garlic, dill or salt.
components.why: It is the plate's idea, on the writer's reading and not the chef's statement: smoked meat on rye is the Montreal deli sandwich, and this plate sets the deli's spice and the deli's bread, as a tuile, around a French tartare. Caraway is the link: it is the seasoning of rye bread.

components.name: Caraway (in the Montreal seasoning)
components.what: The dried fruit, called a seed, of Carum carvi, a plant of the carrot family native to Europe.
components.how: Used whole or cracked in the blend.
components.tastes: Warm, a little sharp, anise-like: the flavor most people think of as rye bread. One teaching source credits the compound D-carvone; a second copy names anethole, so only the taste is claimed here.
components.why: It ties the spice to the tuile. Rye the grain is earthy and malty; the deli rye taste is caraway. On this plate the grain is in the wafer and the caraway is in the seasoning.

components.name: Coriander seed, chili flake and mustard seed (in the Montreal seasoning)
components.what: Coriander seed is the dried fruit of the plant whose leaf is cilantro; chili flake is crushed dried red chili; mustard seed is the whole seed that mustard is ground from.
components.how: Cracked or left whole in the blend.
components.tastes: Coriander seed is floral and lemony; chili flake gives a sharp heat at the front of the mouth; mustard seed turns pungent when it is crushed between the teeth.
components.why: Coriander and mustard seed are the pickling spice side of the blend, the part that comes from the smoked meat cure; the chili flake is its heat. Nothing was searched on chili flake itself today.

components.name: Vital Farms egg yolk
components.what: A yolk from Vital Farms, the pasture-raised egg company the sheet names; the same name is printed on the breakfast hanger steak's egg.
components.how: The sheet lists it on its own, apart from the yolk in the dressing. In the classic it sits raw on top of the beef, to be broken and stirred in. Whether ours is raw, and where it sits, is not printed; the producer says its eggs in the shell are not pasteurized.
components.tastes: Rich, round and coating; a hen that forages tends to lay a deeper orange yolk.
components.why: It is the sauce the guest makes at the table: broken over the beef it adds fat and gloss and softens the mustard and spice. It is also a raw egg question, so it falls under the consumer advisory with the beef, and under the service note for egg.

components.name: Rye tuile
components.what: A tuile is a thin, crisp wafer; the word is French for a roof tile, after the curved shape the classic takes. Most are sweet, made of sugar, egg whites, butter and flour; savory ones are made too, and this one is made with rye.
components.how: A classic tuile batter is spread or piped very thin, baked, and shaped while still warm, because it sets hard as it cools (a minute back in the oven softens one that set too soon). The house recipe, its flour, fat and egg, is not printed.
components.tastes: Crisp and snapping, with rye's earthy, malty grain flavor.
components.why: Every tartare wants something crisp beside it; the brasserie answer is toast or fries, and this is the kitchen's answer, in the grain of the Montreal deli's bread. Rye is a gluten grain and the sheet marks Gluten; dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

products.name: Vital Farms
products.kind: an egg company and its network of farms
products.what: A company founded in 2007 near Austin, Texas, that sells pasture-raised eggs from a network of contracted small family farms: 575 by its own count in November 2025, more than 600 by the end of that year. Its standard is at least 108 square feet of outdoor pasture a hen, the Certified Humane figure. It is a public company and a Certified B Corporation. Its eggs in the shell are not pasteurized; its liquid egg is.

products.name: Montreal seasoning (Montreal steak spice)
products.what: A dry steak spice from the smoked meat delis of Montreal, built on the pickling spices of the smoked meat rub. There is no one recipe: the common commercial blend is garlic, coriander, black pepper, cayenne flakes, dill seed and salt, one maker's page lists caraway, thyme and lemon as well, and the house's is the five on the sheet. Schwartz's bottles its own Steak & Beef Spice and, by CBC's report, sells more than a thousand bottles a week.

products.name: Schwartz's, the Montreal Hebrew Delicatessen
products.what: The smoked meat deli the sheet names, opened on 31 December 1928 by a Jewish immigrant from Romania and still trading. The steak spice story is set at its grill in the 1940s and 1950s. The sheet's 'Hebrew Delicatessan' is this place; the spelling is delicatessen.

products.name: Dijon
products.kind: a style of mustard named for a town in Burgundy
products.what: Smooth, pale, sharp mustard of brown seed. The pack's mustard card already carries the history (the modern style from 1856, a name that is not protected and can be made anywhere); nothing was added to it today, and which mustard the kitchen buys is not printed.

products.name: Le Guide Culinaire
products.what: Auguste Escoffier's kitchen manual for professional cooks, first published in 1903, with later editions in 1907, 1912 and 1921; the book where both early versions of this dish are written down.

guestQuestions.answer: Yes. Raw beef tenderloin, cut and dressed, never cooked, and there is egg yolk with it. Say so before the order, with the consumer advisory.

guestQuestions.asked: Is it okay to eat raw beef?
guestQuestions.answer: Never promise that it carries no risk. The code lets a restaurant serve steak tartare at the guest's own choice, with the reminder that raw or undercooked meats and eggs may increase the risk of foodborne illness; the USDA's own advice is that only cooking kills the bacteria raw beef can carry. Give the advisory, let the guest decide, and send any health question to the manager or the kitchen.

guestQuestions.asked: Is the egg raw too? Is it pasteurized?
guestQuestions.answer: There is yolk in the dressing and a separate yolk. Vital Farms says its eggs in the shell are not pasteurized, and the sheet does not say how the kitchen handles the yolk, so the honest answer is: I will check with the kitchen. Never say pasteurized on a guess. A raw yolk is one of the foods the consumer advisory is written for.
Warm and aromatic more than hot: black pepper and a little chili flake in the Montreal seasoning, and a touch of hot sauce in the dressing. How much heat tonight is the kitchen's answer.

guestQuestions.asked: Is it like a raw hamburger?
guestQuestions.answer: No. The classic is a whole cut, trimmed and diced by hand into small cubes, not mince, so it eats clean and silky, and it is seasoned like a sauce: yolk, mustard, capers, shallot. (How our kitchen cuts it is a lineup question.)

guestQuestions.asked: Why is it called tartare? Is it from the Tartars?
guestQuestions.answer: The name comes from tartar sauce. A century ago the dish was beefsteak à l'Américaine; a version served with tartar sauce was steak à la tartare, and the name stuck to the whole dish. The story about horsemen keeping meat under their saddles is a legend.

guestQuestions.asked: So is there tartar sauce on it?
guestQuestions.answer: No. The dressing is egg yolk and Dijon with capers, shallot, parsley, pepper and hot sauce. Tartar sauce is a cold sauce of the mayonnaise family; the two share a name and a few ingredients, nothing more.

guestQuestions.asked: What is Montreal seasoning? Is it the one from the grocery store?
guestQuestions.answer: Same family, different blend. It is the steak spice of Montreal's smoked meat delis, said to have started at Schwartz's when a grill cook used the smoked meat pickling spices on his own steaks. The store blend leans on garlic, dill and salt; ours is the five on the sheet: black pepper, caraway, coriander, chili flake and mustard seed.

guestQuestions.asked: What is the rye? Is it rye bread?
guestQuestions.answer: A rye tuile, TWEEL: a thin, crisp wafer, named for the French roof tile, made here with rye. It is there for crunch. The taste people expect from rye bread is caraway, and that is in the seasoning, so the two meet on the plate.

Because nothing gets cooked, the cut has to be tender on its own, and tenderloin is the most tender cut there is: lean, fine-grained, mild. It is the classic choice (the French call the dish tartare de filet de boeuf), though some cooks use rump for a beefier taste.

guestQuestions.asked: What happened to the tartare cannoli?
guestQuestions.answer: It has come off the menu and this plate replaces it. This one has no potato shell, no crème fraîche and no cured, grated yolk: it is the classic form, dressed beef with a whole yolk and something crisp beside it.

guestQuestions.asked: Can I have it without the egg, or cooked?
guestQuestions.answer: That is the kitchen's call, not mine: egg is in the dressing as well as the separate yolk, so taking the yolk off does not take egg out of the plate. I ask the kitchen before I answer.
An egg company from Austin, Texas, that works with hundreds of small family farms; its hens are pasture-raised, each with at least 108 square feet of outdoor pasture.

mixUps.tell: The first is the raw beef dish; the second is a cold sauce of the mayonnaise family for fried fish. The dish got its name from the sauce (steak à la tartare, steak with tartar sauce) and then lost the sauce. Ours has none.

À l'Américaine has the raw egg yolk and the capers, onion and parsley. À la Tartare is the same beef without the yolk, with tartar sauce on the side. Today's steak tartare is the first one under the second one's name.

mixUps.b: Steak Tartare Cannoli (a past menu item)
mixUps.tell: With Rye: dressed beef, Montreal seasoning, a whole yolk, a rye tuile. The Cannoli: tartare piped into a fried potato shell with crème fraîche and a cured, grated yolk. If a guest asks for the tartare cannoli, it has gone.

mixUps.b: The cured yolk (egg yolk bottarga) of the old cannoli
mixUps.tell: A cured yolk is salted and dried until firm enough to grate. This plate lists a plain Vital Farms egg yolk; whether it is served raw is the kitchen's answer.

They sound alike and mean different things. Pasture-raised is how the hens live (outdoors, 108 square feet each); pasteurized is a heat treatment of the egg. Vital Farms eggs are the first and, in the shell, by the company's own word, not the second.

mixUps.b: The grocery store Montreal steak seasoning
mixUps.tell: Ours is the sheet's five: black pepper, caraway, coriander, chili flake, mustard seed. The familiar commercial blend is garlic, coriander, black pepper, cayenne flakes, dill seed and salt. Say only our five.
Rye the grain is earthy and malty. The anise-like taste of a deli rye loaf is caraway seed. Here the rye is in the tuile and the caraway is in the seasoning.

Smoked meat is the cured, spiced and smoked beef of the Montreal deli. The steak spice is the dry blend that grew out of that cure's pickling spices and went onto steaks. Our plate borrows the spice, not the meat.

The classic tartare is diced with a knife so the pieces stay separate and clean; ground beef smears. The dictionary still says ground beef, so a guest may picture mince. How ours is cut is a lineup ask.

mixUps.b: Vital Farms as a farm or a co-op
mixUps.tell: It is one company buying from hundreds of contracted family farms that follow its standard, not a single farm and not a cooperative owned by the farmers.

pairingLogic.firstPick: Damien Martin Bourgogne Pinot Noir 2023 (w-y0ihoyc7), the pack's first pick; this file adds only the reasoning about the style.

lines.text: A tartare has no char and little fat, so it has nothing to soften tannin. Pairing writers send it to light reds with little tannin, Gamay from Beaujolais and young Pinot Noir from Burgundy first, sometimes Cabernet Franc, and warn that a strong or tannic wine overwhelms it.
Acidity is the other half: a fresh wine cuts the yolk's richness and stands up to mustard and capers, which is also why a dry sparkling wine or a crisp white is the usual alternative to a light red.
The glass sheet's own words for this wine fit that brief: strawberry, black cherry and raspberry, silky tannins, the fruit from the Mâconnais in southern Burgundy.

sources.title: Tartar sauce
sources.supports: Citing the Wikisource transcription of the 1903 Guide: Beefsteak à la Tartare is the à l'Américaine preparation without the egg yolk on top, with sauce tartare served separately. Escoffier's 1903 sauce tartare: hard-boiled egg yolks worked to a paste, mounted with oil and vinegar, finished with a puree of green onion or chives and a little mayonnaise.

sources.title: Steak tartare
sources.supports: In the early twentieth century the dish was called steack à l'Americaine in Europe; the 1921 edition of the Guide defines steack à la tartare as the à l'Americaine made without egg yolk, tartar sauce on the side; steak à la tartare, literally served with tartar sauce, was later shortened to steak tartare; the 1938 Larousse Gastronomique describes steak tartare as raw ground beef with a raw egg yolk and no tartar sauce; the saddle story, with the Cambridge Medieval History's account that the meat was laid there for the horses' sores.

sources.title: steak tartare
sources.supports: A standard reference work. Raw chopped beef began appearing on a few French bistro and restaurant menus in the late 19th century and was common in the early 20th; it was at first called à l'Américaine, in the American style, presumably because popular belief held that Americans ate meat raw; Escoffier's Guide of 1903 included Beefsteak à l'Américaine; tartare refers to the Tatar people of Central Asia; the classic is chopped raw beefsteak bound by raw egg yolk and seasoned with mustard, capers and other ingredients. Its short entry runs Escoffier's two dishes together (it puts the tartar sauce beside the à l'Américaine).

sources.title: steak tartare (dictionary entry)
sources.supports: A standard reference work. Definition: highly seasoned ground beef eaten raw. Etymology: French tartare, Tartar. First known use in English: 1911.

sources.title: Tartar (dictionary entry)
sources.supports: A standard reference work. Tartar: in English since the 14th century, from Middle French Tartare, probably from Medieval Latin Tartarus, a modification of Persian Tātār.

sources.title: Steak Tartare
sources.supports: Reports a raw dish called Hamburg Steak à la tartare in The Epicurean (1894) by Charles Ranhofer, and notes that the Merriam-Webster date for steak tartare is only 1911.

The summary could not settle whether that version is served raw or how it is sauced. The scan of the book is archive.org item epicureancomplet00ranhrich.

sources.title: Hamburg steak
sources.supports: Hamburg steak was popular in New York in the late 19th century; the oldest English document that names it is a Delmonico's menu of 1873, a dish developed by Charles Ranhofer.

sources.title: The Steak Tartare Warrior Myth You Have To Stop Believing

sources.title: Montreal steak seasoning
sources.supports: Dated to about the 1940s; based on the pickling dry rub of Montreal smoked meat; the account that a broilerman at Schwartz's, known as The Shadow, in the 1940s and 1950s began adding the deli's smoked meat pickling spices to his own rib and liver steaks, that customers asked for the same, and that Moishes Steakhouse and the Main Deli Steak House came to spice their steaks the same way; main ingredients garlic, coriander, black pepper, cayenne pepper flakes, dill seed and salt.

sources.title: Schwartz's
sources.supports: Established on 31 December 1928 by a Jewish immigrant from Romania; also known as the Montreal Hebrew Delicatessen; repeats the broilerman account of the steak spice.

sources.title: 'Tis the seasoning: What's behind Montreal steak spice, flavouring food for more than 70 years?
sources.supports: Credits a cook at Schwartz's known as The Shadow, who worked there decades ago, with popularizing the mixture; its sub-headline says only he knows the real origins; Schwartz's sells more than a thousand bottles of its Steak & Beef Spice a week. The article's date did not show in the search.

sources.title: Spices (course handout, spices1.pdf)

A second copy of a similar handout names anethole for caraway instead, so the compound is not settled here.
